example: Simple multiple-choice questions ("What year did Darwin publish On the Origin of Species?").
Translate a sentence between two languages.
Entity classification.
Beating Stockfish at chess.
Arithmetic problems.
Solving a Sudoku.
Theorem proving of the Poincaré conjecture.
Navigation tasks such as driving from JFK airport to the centre of Manhattan.
Writing the "Silo" novels.
Design a house.
Playing strategy board games such as Monopoly or Diplomacy.
Participating in a cooperative board game like Pandemic, where all players share objectives and known roles.
Multi-party negotiation with fixed payoffs or structured debates.
Developing a long-term exercise routine tailored to a single person's fitness goals.
Negotiate the settlement of a copyright-infringement legal case, where each party's objectives are clear but interactions are intricate.
Coordinate a team to carry out a research project.
Managing air-traffic control for an airport: coordinating many flights and pilots with known procedures but complex timing.
Lead a fast-growing startup in a quickly growing and competitive market.
Infiltrate or disrupt an adversarial organisation.
Commanding a large-scale emergency response during an unfolding natural disaster, such as a major earthquake with cascading aftershocks and infrastructure failures.
Coordinating humanitarian-aid distribution in a conflict zone, balancing unknown local actors and rapidly changing conditions.
Navigating a company's response to sudden regulatory changes while competing firms exploit the situation.
Solving a complex mathematical proof (e.g., working on the Riemann hypothesis).
Transcribing a recorded audio lecture into text.
Optimising a supply chain using a deterministic model.
Ordering food by phone or at a café.
Asking a librarian for the location of a specific book.
Scheduling a haircut or dental appointment via chat.
Bargaining in a foreign market with unfamiliar norms.
Explaining the rules of a complex board game (e.g., Twilight Imperium) to a group of first-time players from a different cultural background.
Participating in a first business meeting with partners from a high-context culture where implicit cues matter.
Explaining to supporters why a political party or sports team suffered a loss.
Mediating a heated argument between two colleagues over the office thermostat.
Giving constructive but critical feedback to a friend or colleague about a minor performance issue.
Resolving a dispute about shared property (e.g., which roommate gets the larger bedroom).
A commander informing a family that a soldier died in service.
A manager informing an employee of termination or major performance issues.
A doctor delivering a serious diagnosis (e.g., cancer) and discussing options.
A teacher discussing serious behavioural concerns with a student's parents.
Negotiating the release of hostages held by a fundamentalist group known for violence and unpredictability.
Negotiating the custody of children in a divorce where the parties are very upset with each other.
Chairing a tense international climate summit to forge a binding agreement between nations with conflicting economic and political interests.
Conducting crisis communication for a public-health emergency across diverse communities with varying beliefs.
Solve a Sudoku from a printed grid. (The whole state is given; filling the grid is deduction and planning.)
Find the winning plan in a chess position shown on the board. (Nothing is hidden; the demand is Planning.)
Answer a word problem that states every quantity it needs: two trains leave stations 300 km apart at given speeds, and you must say when they meet.
Check a museum's opening hours before planning a visit.
Read the current contents of a file before editing it.
Measure the floor of a room with a tape before ordering a carpet for it.
Explore an unfamiliar codebase to establish where a behaviour is implemented, each file being directly readable.
Look up a customer's account, orders and reservations across several systems before making a change.
Take a complete inventory of a storeroom, however many shelves it holds — each item is simply there to be counted.

Debug why a program you did not write crashes: the whole source is there to read, but no line of it announces the fault — only its symptoms are visible, and experiments must be devised to expose it. (Tracing a fault back through work the solver produced itself is not situational understanding, however long it stayed unnoticed.)
Locate a fault in an electrical circuit using a multimeter.
Work out why a houseplant is dying from its appearance and conditions.

Drive through dense city traffic, where the situation changes continuously but every change is visible as it happens. (Other drivers' visible motion is tracked state; reasoning about their intentions is Mind Modelling (MSm).)
Monitor a staged software rollout across services, where dashboards show each service's changing state.
Cook several dishes at once, each evolving visibly toward done or ruined.
Diagnose an intermittent fault that appears and disappears under conditions that cannot be observed directly, such as a race condition.
Navigate at sea by dead reckoning in fog, where position evolves unobserved under wind and current.
Fight a building fire that spreads unseen behind walls and ceilings, revealing itself only intermittently.
Prove that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
Transcribe a recorded lecture into text.
Find the cheapest combination of flights for a fixed itinerary.
Order a coffee and a sandwich at a café counter.
Ask a librarian which shelf holds a book you can name.
Message a dental practice to move an appointment from Tuesday to Thursday.

Write a newspaper column arguing for a national carbon tax. (However hard the argument is to make, it is composed and sent with no exchange to steer: choosing the words is Verbal Expression, judging what the readership already believes is Mind Modelling (MSm).)
Take a patient's history in a clinic, where each answer determines which symptom to ask about next.
Interview a job candidate about a project on their CV, following up on what they actually say rather than reading out fixed questions.
Work out over a support chat which of several products a customer actually needs, each follow-up question depending on what they have just said.
Tell a colleague that the section they wrote for a shared report has to be rewritten before submission, when they are proud of it but will hear you out.

Tell a patient, as their doctor, that they have a serious illness, and bring them to accept a treatment they are at first reluctant to start, working through each concern as it is raised. (Grave and emotionally heavy, but they are not holding out for a different treatment — the work is finding the path to acceptance, not overcoming opposition.)
Settle a dispute between two flatmates over the cleaning rota, where each arrived wanting a different split and both will accept whatever they come to see as fair.
Agree a price with a market trader who opens far above what you will pay, where both of you want the sale to happen and the work is finding the figure that suits you both.
Persuade a landlord to release you from a lease six months early, when they have no reason to agree and would rather keep collecting the rent.
Keep refusing a refund the policy does not allow to a customer who is shouting and demanding a manager, without conceding it and without the exchange breaking down.
Talk a co-founder out of a launch date they have staked their reputation on and still believe in.

Negotiate a hostage release in which the captor, the police commander pressing to storm the building, and the hostages' families each demand a different course, and each of them reads what is conceded to the others.
Chair the closing night of a treaty negotiation where three delegations have stated public red lines that cannot all be honoured.
Settle the custody arrangement in a divorce where both parents want the child to live with them and each expects the other to exploit any concession.
